newsitem.title: USA: USDA's Glickman says EEP in USDA's arsenal.
newsitem.headline: USDA's Glickman says EEP in USDA's arsenal.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman Tuesday said that the Export Enhancement Program was in the department's "arsenal" but that to date subsidies by the European Union have not been "material."
"The EU use of these subsidies to date has not been material. We have to watch what they're doing, it's in our arsenal to deal with..." he said in an interview.
Glickman said USDA did not want to restart a subsidy war but repeated his determination to act if necessary.
"We will do our best to resist efforts to get involved unless we have to to protect our markets and our farmers and that will depend upon what the EU does."
"Right now we are not poised to move tomorrow on this thing," he said, but added "we will be ready to act if we need to."
Glickman said it was not likely aggressive sales by Australia and Argentina in the months ahead might trigger use of the EEP. Both countries are seen having large stocks on hand to export.

"I doubt that you would see those actions triggering EEP. They're (Australia and Argentina) just not that big a long-term factor in the marketplace. We hope that those sales are market oriented and to the extent that they are not I'm sure that they will hear from us," he said.
The secretary cited tight U.S. wheat stocks as another disincentive for using the subsidy program now. But he said a larger wheat crop next year would make it easier to use EEP.
"The higher the stocks we have the more ability we have to use the program," Glickman said.

Glickman noted that Congress has only allocated $100 million for EEP in the current budget but said the department would not seek additional funding for the program until it had made the decision to restart it.
He remarked that he has been "amazed" by the media focus on the subsidy issue and said "it doesn't dominate our thinking at all."
Glickman said he left Monday's meeting between top EU officials and President Clinton "somewhat encouraged" that genetically altered corn would be approved by the EU.
An EU panel is expected to issue an decision on the controversial product later this week.
Glickman and his senior trade advisor Paul Drazek said that the U.S. may be able to legally challenge an EU ban on BT corn if the decision is not based on sound science.
